title: The Theory and Practice of MAP Inference over Non-Convex Constraints
claim: Our solver finds the true optimum under hard constraints quickly, while gradient baselines are imprecise or invalid and exact solvers time out.
layout: 2 panels: constraint map left, accuracy-vs-time scatter right; shared marker legend below
description: Two-part figure with a shared legend of method markers along the bottom. The left panel is a 2-D map of a density heatmap (purple to green, with green as the peak). Pink hatched polygons mark forbidden regions, so the constraint is non-convex. A purple circle marks the target optimum, and the orange star for the proposed method sits on it. Other markers sit elsewhere: a pink up-triangle (Adam) and a down-triangle (PCAdam) lie near the green ridge, and a green X (OptiMathSAT) lies far away in a hatched corner. The right panel is a log-log scatter of relative optimality gap against time. The orange star is alone at the bottom, with a gap near 1e-6 at about 0.5 s. PCAdam sits near 1e-1. OptiMathSAT sits at the top beside a dashed timeout line. A shaded 'Invalid' strip above holds Adam and CDCL-OCAC.
caption: \textbf{{Our structure-aware solver \pamap{} is able to correctly and efficiently perform MAP inference over non-convex constraints and non-log-concave densities}} while classical optimizers (Adam), even when being constrained-aware (\pcadam{}; [ref]), are imprecise and slower and when exact solvers (OptiMathSAT [ref] and CDCL-OCAC [ref]) timeout. If the density factorizes as a tree, our \mpmap{} solver ([ref]) can be exact and even faster (see [ref]).
abstract: In many safety-critical settings, probabilistic ML systems have to make predictions subject to algebraic constraints, e.g., predicting the most likely trajectory that does not cross obstacles. These real-world constraints are rarely convex, nor the densities considered are (log-)concave. This makes computing this constrained maximum a posteriori (MAP) prediction efficiently and reliably extremely challenging. In this paper, we first investigate under which conditions we can perform constrained MAP inference over continuous variables exactly and efficiently and devise a scalable message-passing algorithm for this tractable fragment. Then, we devise a general constrained MAP strategy that interleaves partitioning the domain into convex feasible regions with numerical constrained optimization. We evaluate both methods on synthetic and real-world benchmarks, showing our approaches outperform constraint-agnostic baselines, and scale to complex densities intractable for SoTA exact solvers.
